title: Vivekananda's drunk monkey
hook: a monk in New York tells Americans their mind is a drunk monkey, then defines yoga
carry: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings
tomorrow: when the lake goes still, who is looking?

segments.voice: Yesterday, atha, now: Patanjali fell into open hands, and his book opens the teaching for someone who has arrived.

New York, 1895. A young monk from Calcutta, Swami Vivekananda, has taken rooms in the city and is teaching small classes to Americans who have barely heard the word yoga. He doesn't start with poses. He tells them about a monkey. A monkey is restless by nature. Now someone gives it wine, so it's drunk. Then a scorpion stings it. Then a demon gets into it. That, he says, is the human mind: drunk on desire, stung by jealousy, seized by pride. And the line he keeps coming back to is Patanjali's second.
screen: `NEW YORK, 1895.` → `A RESTLESS MONKEY.` → `DRUNK, STUNG, POSSESSED.` → `THAT'S THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Here it is: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Chitta is the mind in the widest sense: thinking, feeling, remembering. Vritti means a turning, a whirl, from a root that means to turn, like a wheel: the thoughts, the moods, the commentary that never stops. Nirodha means stilling, restraining, bringing to rest. Four words, and not one is about the body. That's the heart of yoga as a Hindu teaching: it's a discipline of the mind. Posture gets only a few threads in the whole book, and most poses taught in classes today grew up much later. Vivekananda gave his students a second picture, a lake. When wind ripples it, you can't see the bottom. When the water goes still, you see all the way down. Why would a Hindu want to see the bottom? Because of what's under the ripples. Patanjali calls it the seer; the Upanishads call it atman, the self. Nirodha can be read as restraint, even cessation, but many teachers hear it as a settling, water going still, not a lid slammed down. And the drunk monkey isn't hopeless. Vivekananda's advice: don't fight it. Let it jump, and watch. Day by day, he said, it gets calmer.
screen: `YOGAŚ CITTA-VṚTTI-NIRODHAḤ.` · `CHITTA, VRITTI, NIRODHA: MIND, TURNING, STILL.` · `NOT ONE WORD ABOUT THE BODY.` · `A LAKE WITH NO WIND.` · `UNDER THE RIPPLES: THE SEER.` · then, large: `YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE MIND'S TURNINGS.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the monkey jump: don't chase it and don't scold it, just watch where it goes, a text, a sound, a small worry. Picture each one as wind on a lake, crossing the surface and passing, and when the water is flat for a moment between them, rest there. If you pray, you can let that stillness be your prayer; if you don't, let it simply be quiet.
Vritti, a turning of the mind. Yoga is the stilling of these turnings: chitta, vritti, nirodha. Mind, turning, stillness.
Your line: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Not your toes. The monkey. Day two ninety-six.

howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often memorize 1.2 in Sanskrit, and many yoga teachers in India and abroad quote it as the definition of yoga before teaching any posture.
